title: How ice and rock triggered Nepal’s catastrophic flood – and why climate change is raising the risks - resilience.org
description: How ice and rock triggered Nepal’s catastrophic flood – and why climate change is raising the risks  resilience.org
publisher.title: resilience.org
full_article:
The catastrophic flood that killed hundreds of people in Nepal on Aug. 26, 2026, and left many more missing likely began with falling ice and rock crashing into the river below, but that wasn’t the end of the disaster. Days later, a new lake pooled behind the debris and then burst, sending more water streaming through the valley.

The destruction represents two of the ways rising temperatures, thawing permafrost and melting ice are increasing the risk of destructive floods in the Himalayas and other high mountain regions around the world.

I am a geologist and part of an ad hoc international group of 50-plus scientists who meet quickly after mountain disasters to analyze satellite images and field data to get information out to the public. This is what we’ve learned so far about the disaster and the region’s rising risks from climate change.

The flood disaster in Nepal

Evidence from satellites and seismic data we have reviewed suggest that an enormous mass of bedrock and glacier ice broke off a slope north of Langtang Lirung and slammed into the valley about 4,000 feet (1,200 meters) below – that’s a distance roughly three times the height of the Eiffel Tower. The landslide shook the earth hard enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 event on seismometers, the U.S. Geological Survey confirmed.

The result was a slurry of melting ice, rock and water that quickly flowed into the river.

We have a rough idea of how much ice fell, and it likely wouldn’t have been enough to trigger the magnitude of the flood that followed. One theory is that the rock and ice briefly dammed the valley, allowing water to back up in the river.

When that blockage broke, a wall of water rushed downstream – reaching towns, taking hundreds of lives and destroying infrastructure. Hundreds more people were stranded by the flood.

Second threat: The lake that formed, then burst

The disaster wasn’t finished when the first wall of water passed. Within a day, authorities warned that a new “barrier lake” estimated to hold a few million cubic meters of water had developed behind avalanche and flood debris where two rivers meet in Tibet, a region of China, before crossing into Nepal.

On Aug. 28, the barrier lake broke its bank and the river rose again. Helicopter search operations were briefly suspended while rescuers and residents on the lower banks scrambled to high ground. The immediate danger eased only when the barrier drained gradually rather than collapsing all at once.

This is the crux of why these events are so dangerous: A temporary, debris-choked dam can form in minutes, hold for hours or days, and fail with little warning. An avalanche-dammed lake often appears and disappears too quickly for conventional monitoring to catch.

Risks are rising

We’re seeing disasters like this happen frequently.

In 2021, a similar rock and ice avalanche in India’s Uttarakhand state sent about 950 million cubic feet (27 million cubic meters) of rock and ice – roughly 80% rock, 20% ice – cascading down from Ronti Peak. It destroyed one hydropower plant, badly damaged another and killed or left missing about 200 people, many of them dam workers.

In 2025, roughly 335 million cubic feet (9.5 million cubic meters) of rock and ice fell from the Birch Glacier in the Swiss Alps, burying most of the village of Blatten; only advance monitoring and the evacuation of more than 300 residents kept the death toll to one.

The number of glacial lakes has also increased around the world, raising the risk of outburst floods. And more mountain slopes are now at risk of landslides than in the past.

In 2023, thawing permafrost led to a rock collapse into South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, India, generating a wave that burst through the moraine holding back the glacial lake. The outburst flood sent more than 13 billion gallons (50 million cubic meters) of water rushing down the mountain, damaging several dams, more than 25,000 buildings and more than 30 bridges.

Climate change is one major contributor to rising disaster risk.

The last 10 years have been the warmest on record globally, and that has accelerated snow and glacier melt.

Populations are growing, too, and these valleys are increasingly being used to generate hydropower. As countries build more infrastructure in these places, the hazard risk rises because more people and development sit in the flood’s path.

The valley where the latest disaster occurred held multiple hydropower plants – Nepal’s electricity authority said the flood knocked about a dozen major generation and transmission facilities offline. Bridges and a major border crossing, the Gyirong Port gateway between Nepal and China, were also destroyed. It became a catastrophe because of where the water, rock and mud landed.

Thawing permafrost, geology raise flood risk

Together with the neighboring Hindu Kush mountains, the rugged Himalayas that stretch across Asia contain one of the world’s largest volumes of ice. They’re sometimes called the “third pole” for that reason.

As temperatures have risen, their ice loss rates roughly doubled since 2000, according to studies from the Nepal-based International Center for Integrated Mountain Development, or ICIMOD.

And it isn’t only the glaciers that are melting. High mountain slopes are also held together by permafrost – ground that stays frozen year-round – with ice filling the cracks and joints in the rock like a natural cement. As that frozen ground warms and ice inside thaws, the cement weakens, and slopes that stood for thousands of years can lose their grip.

Meltwater from snow and ice seeps into cracks in the rock. Where it refreezes, it can pry those cracks wider. Where it stays liquid, it acts as a lubricant along the surfaces where rock and ice meet.

On a steep cliff, these water-filled fractures can sometimes be the difference between a face that holds and one that gives way all at once – sending millions of tons of rock and ice into the valley below in seconds.

Not every thaw ends in disaster. But rising temperatures steadily load the dice: more slopes lose their frozen glue, more meltwater works its way into the cracks, and the odds of a catastrophic collapse rise year after year.

In the 2021 disaster in Uttarakhand, thawing likely contributed to the collapse of a large slab of rock and ice on the face of Ronti Peak.

Early indications in Nepal point to a similar story: a large mass of rock and ice detaching from a mountainside and falling, triggering the August 2026 flood. Comparing satellite images of the site from before and after, first posted by my colleague Dan Shugar, we have also noticed that a lot of snow had disappeared in the days preceding the flood. That snowmelt had to go somewhere – and it may have supplied the water that lubricated the rockfall.

How to lower the risk

From a risk standpoint, some areas of these mountains are extremely dangerous today.

To help protect people, early warning systems are crucial. When a flood starts, people living farther down the valley might have several minutes to get to safety before the water arrives – and minutes are enough to save lives.

Nepal has warning systems in place, and they have been credited with preventing casualties in the past. But the warning systems rely heavily on river-level gauges, which work far better for monsoon floods than for a wall of water moving tens of meters per second – and the flood itself likely destroyed the very gauges the warning systems depend on.

Building redundancy into the system would help, such as adding seismic sensors that detect a large mass movement the instant it happens, sirens and loudspeakers in valley-bottom settlements, radio and satellite-based cell broadcasts that don’t rely on a single tower that a flood can sweep away, and automatic alerts triggered when an avalanche and sudden water and sediment level in the river jumps.

Knowing the risks can also improve permit decisions for hydropower dams, roads and buildings in high-hazard corridors – and it can push monitoring beyond the familiar checklist of large glacial lakes to hanging glaciers, steep ice-and-rock slopes, permafrost, and the short-lived debris dams that can be just as deadly.

Regional cooperation is also important. When rivers cross borders or a transboundary glacial lake has potential to fail, the disaster doesn’t stop at the border. The water that devastated Nepal began on the Tibetan side, and the barrier lake that threatened a second surge sat right on the frontier.

title: Rescuers dig 4 bodies from a Nepal hydropower tunnel as families demand answers - baltimoresun.com
description: Rescuers dig 4 bodies from a Nepal hydropower tunnel as families demand answers  baltimoresun.com
publisher.title: baltimoresun.com
full_article:
By BINAJ GURUBACHARYA

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Rescuers in Nepal have recovered four bodies from the tunnel of a hydropower plant as search operations continued for those still missing three weeks after the devastating flash flood last month that killed hundreds and left thousands missing.

Families of the thousands missing, meanwhile, are seeking answers from authorities on their whereabouts.

Nepal’s army said that four bodies were recovered Wednesday from the Chilime Hydropower plant, which was situated on the Trishuli River that flooded on Aug. 26.

Families of the missing have been pressuring the government to speed up the rescue and recovery process from the tunnels.

They have held rallies and many have called on the government to declare the missing as dead because they want to receive death certificates, which would allow them to move forward with legal proceedings and religious rites and give them some emotional closure.

At the Tribhuvan University Teaching hospital in Kathmandu, the lobby walls have been pasted with photos of hundreds of missing people. Relatives go there seeking news of their loved ones.

Usha Khatri’s husband Indra Bahadur was working as a cook with a group of pilgrims when the flood hit the Nepal-China border. Since then she has been searching for him in many of the towns where the river flows and where bodies have been recovered.

“The government has not done much for us. They have not met us or given any information or any assurances. I am by myself searching for my husband,” Khatri said.

There were 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the flooding and many workers were either swept or trapped by the raging water or debris.

Finding the workers who were trapped has been a priority for the government and rescuers. But access to the tunnels has been hampered by thick mud, debris and damaged infrastructure, making it difficult for rescue teams to reach the areas.

Two Nepali workers were found alive by rescuers on Sept. 4, days after the flooding. A day later a Chinese worker was pulled out alive from a separate area.

The government estimates the country’s reconstruction costs at around $4.78 billion.

title: Processing Nepal’s Heartbreak from a Goshen Apartment - Goshen College
description: Processing Nepal’s Heartbreak from a Goshen Apartment  Goshen College
publisher.title: Goshen College
full_article:
When you grow up in Nepal, the landscape is a part of who you are. Nepal is a place where mountains touch the sky, where green hills wrap around quiet villages and where community is the foundation of daily life. Doors are always left open for neighbors, tea is shared freely and families stick together through everything. It is a very beautiful and colorful country. Despite being separated by thousands of miles when I came here to study at Goshen College, there is no doubt that Nepal always carries a piece of my heart.

In Nepal, monsoon season is always accompanied by large amounts of precipitation. Yet, this year’s rainfall was special in its own way. This disaster took place in northern and central parts of Nepal, which comprise the territories of the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers including the Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan districts. The sudden flash floods covered streets and markets in regions such as Trishuli Bazar and Syabrubesi within just a few hours of rainfall. Roads were washed away entirely, houses were buried in mud, and sudden rivers blocked off the region from any assistance.

Even though it wasn’t the exact town where I grew up, it felt like a part of me was lost in that flood too. When you are living so far away, you realize just how deeply you love your country and how much it hurts to see it in pain.

I was born and raised in Kathmandu — Nepal’s capital city. While Kathmandu sits further south and was spared from the worst of this specific disaster’s destruction, every corner of Nepal is connected by shared rivers, roads and family ties. When a flash flood destroys a bridge in Rasuwa or sweeps through Trishuli Bazar, the shockwave reaches Kathmandu in minutes.

My friends back home were glued to their phones, desperately trying to reach relatives living in mountain villages along the Trishuli corridor. Local market routes closed overnight, supply lines stalled and everyone I knew in Kathmandu was reaching out to check on friends and loved ones caught in the disaster zone. Growing up in Nepal means learning early on that when one region hurts, the whole country feels the pain.

Behind those headlines are real people and families. Thousands of homes were destroyed overnight. Parents lost their children, young kids were suddenly left without parents, and families who already had very little lost every single thing they owned. Pets had no owners left to feed them.

Watching all of this happen from a dorm room in Indiana is a very scary and exhausting feeling. When a disaster hits your home country while you are studying abroad, your world splits in two. On one side, life at GC goes on as normal: you walk to class, sit in the dining hall and do your homework. On the other side, your mind is thousands of miles away.

title: The owner of the Grace Clinic plastic surgery clinic died tragically in Nepal - UA.NEWS
description: The owner of the Grace Clinic plastic surgery clinic died tragically in Nepal  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
It has been reported that Lyudmila Kilyvnik, the owner of the Grace Clinic plastic surgery clinic, died tragically in Nepal.

Her name had previously appeared on the list of Ukrainians being sought following a mudslide in Nepal on August 26. At the time, it was reported that the group was in the area of ​​the route to Mount Kailash.

Lyudmila Kilyvnik entered the world of youth and beauty in 2011 by chance, as she herself recalled during an interview.

“Yes, I have a degree in economics and significant experience in corporate management. I first came to the GRACE Clinic way back in 2011 as a patient—I needed to have my ear stitched up. At that time, the clinic was going through a crisis, and the founder approached me with a request to save it,” she told the likein.ua portal.

Lyudmila agreed to take on this project as a crisis manager.

“This business has become my source of strength; through it, I’ve come to love myself even more. I’m not involved in day-to-day operations (we have a CEO for that), but rather serve as a source of inspiration—a sort of producer for our talented doctors. I also serve as a guarantor for patients through my reputation and good name. And, thank God, in all these years, no one has ever woken me up with an alarm call. This means we’re working in synergy and moving in the right direction,” Lyudmila recalled.

At first, the GRACE clinic specialized in plastic surgery, but over time, the needs and desires of our clients changed, and the clinic evolved alongside them.

“I’m proud that most of the doctors at our clinic have been working here since its founding—almost 15 years. This is a tremendous effort and achievement, something of great value to us—the creation and continuation of traditions. However, growth is impossible without bringing in young doctors, modern technologies, and management systems,” Lyudmila told Forbes.ua.

title: Death toll from floods on Nepal-China border rises to 1,453 — Anadolu Agency - UA.NEWS
description: Death toll from floods on Nepal-China border rises to 1,453 — Anadolu Agency  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
The death toll from flash floods and landslides on the border between Nepal and China has risen to 1,453. Another 6,664 people are considered missing on both sides of the border, Anadolu Agency reports, citing authorities.

Data from Nepal and China

In Nepal, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority reported 1,410 deaths. It also said that 13,756 people had been rescued. The number of missing people in the country stands at 6,145, including 587 foreigners.

On the Chinese side of the border, the death toll remains at 43. Another 519 people are considered missing, including 261 foreigners in Tibet, which Beijing calls the Xizang Autonomous Region.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Cause of the disaster

The disaster occurred on August 26 after a rupture took place on the glacier of Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal at an altitude of 5,200 meters. It triggered an ice-rock avalanche that turned into a large-scale mudflow and passed through valleys along the border.

Floods and landslides devastated Nepal's Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley. In the Xizang Autonomous Region, the mudflow buried the Gyirong border crossing.

title: Global warming slowly brought about the catastrophic collapse of the Nepalese glacier - EL PAÍS English
description: Global warming slowly brought about the catastrophic collapse of the Nepalese glacier  EL PAÍS English
publisher.title: EL PAÍS English
full_article:
The catastrophic avalanche of rock and ice on Langtang Lirung mountain, on Nepal’s northern border — which caused 1,300 deaths and as a result of which, 22 days later, more than 5,000 people remain missing — was the result of a combination of factors that simmered until they triggered an unprecedented disaster in the Himalayas. A report published on September 17 by World Weather Attribution (WWA), the group of scientists that specializes in calculating the influence of climate change on extreme weather events, sheds light on the catastrophe. Among the factors, the authors note “unusually warm conditions before the failure, supporting enhanced snow and ice melt and more precipitation falling as rain rather than snow” around the site where the collapse occurred.

But this story has other protagonists, because “it was not a single triggering event,” explains Professor Walter Immerzeel of Utrecht University, referring to the factors that contributed to the collapse on the mountainside at an altitude of 5,150 meters on August 26. This hydrology expert, who has worked in the area for years and is one of the WWA report’s authors, says those factors “acted together over” years and decades. To global warming he adds an earthquake that struck the region in April 2015 and “may have preconditioned the slope” for failure. “The earthquake had a magnitude of 7.8 and also caused widespread devastation in Nepal, triggering numerous landslides in the country’s central region,” he adds. Scientists suspect that quake “may have weakened the rock mass” beneath the glacier.

The collapse unleashed a massive flood of water, ice and debris that swept downstream, causing catastrophic damage. Immerzeel says it was “an unprecedented disaster in the Himalayas”: “The mechanism behind this disaster is comparable to the one in India’s Uttarakhand, known as the Chamoli disaster [a glacier collapse that occurred in February 2021]. But the mass that fell there was roughly one-fifth of the mass that fell this time, and the impact was also much smaller.”

In the recent Nepal disaster, the glacier’s failure triggered a rock-and-ice avalanche that grew as it descended the river channel. “A wall of water, ice, rock and sediment reached the Rasuwagadhi border, 22 km downstream, within seven minutes, moving at an average speed of 188 km per hour, and wiped out the border facilities, the town of Timure and the Syabrubesi market town within the next quarter of an hour, catching pilgrims, border staff and hydropower workers,” the WWA report recounts.

“The resulting debris flood was therefore likely caused by several sources of water, including melting glacier ice, water stored beneath the glacier and in permafrost, ice and water carried within the debris, and river water pushed ahead of the flow,” the analysis summarizes. That water volume was augmented by heavy precipitation that fell in the area in October and November 2025 as snow. When temperatures rose in the following months, that snow turned to water, fueling the disaster.

Climate change

The heat that arrived with summer was also abnormal. July and August temperatures were “substantially warmer” than the local average, the study says. The fingerprint of climate change is visible there, but also in the year‑by‑year glacier melt. “Glaciers across this region have thinned by roughly half a meter a year since 2000, and the glacier next to the slope that collapsed retreated more than 300 meters between 2010 and 2026,” Immerzeel explains. “The presence of that glacier is very important because it basically buttresses the rock face,” he adds.

Moreover, warming has “shifted to higher elevations consistent with global warming,” which can “contribute to the degradation of high-elevation permafrost, glacial thinning and retreat, the snowfall-rainfall transition, and associated slope instability,” the report warns. The researchers estimate the freezing threshold is rising about 100 meters per decade. In other words, during the monsoon and post‑monsoon seasons, the zero degrees Celsius line climbs roughly 100 meters up the mountain each decade.

The problem is that this threshold is not exceeded year‑round but varies with the seasons. That increases “the number of freeze‑thaw cycles.” “Water becomes liquid and then refreezes, which exerts all kinds of stress on fractures” in the rock, Immerzeel notes.

“There is no doubt that climate change is one of the factors that drove the disaster,” says Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London and co‑founder of WWA. In her view, this link must “be discussed in the context of losses and damages” related to climate change.

For years, the countries most vulnerable to climate impacts — which are also often the least responsible for the problem — have been urging the UN to set up a compensation mechanism that would require the wealthiest and highest fossil fuel‑consuming states to pay. In May, the UN General Assembly took a symbolic step in that direction by approving a resolution sponsored by Vanuatu, a small Pacific island republic, calling on states that fail to meet their climate obligations to offer restitution to nations hardest hit by warming. The measure passed with the support of 141 countries despite active opposition from the United States and a group of oil‑producing states led by Saudi Arabia. But the resolution was nonbinding, and that commitment needs to be carried into climate treaties.

full_article:
When an immense and inexorable flow of rock, mud and water barreled through northern Nepal on August 26, it killed more than 1,200 people and left thousands still missing. The magnitude of the event caught even experts on the region’s geology off guard.

“The victims, their pain and all the ruined towns … it is almost impossible to believe,” says geological engineer Ranjan Dahal of Tribhuvan University in Kathmandu, Nepal, who has studied geohazards in the Himalaya for nearly 30 years. “I don’t think even Hollywood could make such a movie.”

title: Photos: Villages in Nepal remain buried in mud 3 weeks after deadly flood - Yahoo
description: Photos: Villages in Nepal remain buried in mud 3 weeks after deadly flood  Yahoo
publisher.title: Yahoo
full_article:
Nearly three weeks after a catastrophic flash flood tore through northern Nepal, survivors are still shoveling mud from homes and businesses while entire communities remain buried beneath debris.

New visuals from the disaster zone show families living in temporary tent camps, residents wading through mud-filled buildings and volunteers hauling away wreckage by hand. In some villages, broken homes stand empty beside streets covered in boulders, shattered concrete and household belongings.

A view of the destruction following the devastating flash floods on August 26 that struck Devighat, Nuwakot, Nepal, on September 15, 2026. People in the affected areas of Nuwakot continue to return in search of their destroyed homes and the last remaining memories of their lives. (Photo by Abdul Goni/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Devighat, a commercial center about 37 miles northwest of Kathmandu, remains among the hardest-hit communities. Photos show mud stains reaching as high as the fourth floor of some buildings, while collapsed walls and exposed foundations show the force of the Aug. 26 flood.

Aftermath of devastating flash floods that struck Nepal on August 26 is seen in Nuwakot, where people in the affected areas continue to return to the ruins of their homes, searching for belongings and the last remnants of lives that were swept away, in Bagmati province, central Nepal, on September 14, 2026. (Photo by Abdul Goni/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Many residents are unable to return home because structures must first be inspected. Some families are sheltering in tents erected at a nearby school.

Nepal government and various non-governmental organizations provide temporary shelters and assistance to families affected by the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal on August 26, in Devighat Dham, Nuwakot, Nepal, on September 15, 2026. Several temporary shelters are set up along the Galchi-Trishuli-Rasuwagadhi road in Nuwakot, where various organizations and individuals provide food, cooking supplies and other essential items to affected families. (Photo by Abdul Goni/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The cleanup has drawn volunteers from across Nepal. Groups of teachers, students and other residents have traveled from Kathmandu and surrounding areas to dig thick silt from salvageable buildings. Fifty teachers from one secondary school spent a day clearing hardware stores and multistory buildings in Devighat, according to The Straits Times.

A woman clears mud following the devastating flash floods on August 26 that struck Devighat, Nuwakot, Nepal, on September 15, 2026. People in the affected areas of Nuwakot continue to return in search of their destroyed homes and the last remaining memories of their lives. Some are trying to recover essential belongings from the rubble, while others are working with family members to remove soil from parts of their homes buried underground and make them habitable again. (Photo by Abdul Goni/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The work remains dangerous. Buildings weakened by water and debris can collapse without warning, while search teams fear more victims could be buried beneath the mud. Damaged roads and bridges are also slowing the delivery of equipment and supplies to isolated communities.

The disaster began when a massive section of glacier and rock collapsed from Langtang Lirung mountain near Nepal's border with Tibet. An avalanche of snow, ice and rock rushed into the valley, generating a fast-moving flood filled with mud and debris that swept downstream through communities along the Trishuli River.

The flood destroyed homes, settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower facilities. Preliminary assessments indicate that Nepal may need to rebuild approximately 20,000 homes, including about 7,500 that were completely washed away or buried, Reuters reported.

title: The Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: a spur to action on climate | Editorial - The Guardian
description: The Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: a spur to action on climate | Editorial  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
F ollowing a familiar pattern, coverage of the glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border three weeks ago has subsided with the initial shock. But while the world’s attention has shifted, Nepal remains in the midst of an appalling tragedy. As well as at least 1,300 people who are known to have been killed, more than 5,000 are missing, some of them trapped in tunnels linked to the 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the floods. On Wednesday four bodies were recovered from one of these tunnels, with searches ongoing. Families of the missing people are desperate for news.

Last week the country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said that it would ask the UN’s loss and damage fund for $20m (£15m) towards a total rebuilding cost of around $5bn (£3.75bn) – including the replacement of up to 20,000 homes. The first academic study linking the disaster to the climate crisis will now be added to that application. Scientists at Imperial College London, along with international collaborators on the World Weather Attribution project, found that a number of drivers of the glacier fall had been made worse by atmospheric heating. While not the sole cause, fossil fuel pollution was judged to have destabilised the geology of the mountain environment.

View image in fullscreen Shisir Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister. Photograph: Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images

Even before last month, Nepal faced huge economic challenges, due in part to instability in the Middle East. Its government has only been in power for six months, following protests that led to the collapse of the previous one. But inexperienced though they are, Nepal’s leaders are right to insist that other countries should pay towards its recovery. Nepal is estimated to be responsible for less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Like the small island nations in the Caribbean and Pacific that are most threatened by sea level rises and tropical storms, Nepal’s people are bearing the brunt of destructive forces that have been unleashed upon them as a result of decisions about resource use, energy and economic development taken elsewhere in the world.

The likelihood of any payment being made quickly is, however, low. Nearly 120 countries have already submitted claims adding up to a total of nearly $3bn (£2.2bn), which is far more than the fund, currently estimated at $400m (£300m), can afford. That is partly the fault of Donald Trump, who withdrew the US from the Paris climate agreement and put pressure on the World Bank to drop its climate finance goals. Other donors have also failed to meet targets.

The Nepal-Tibet disaster, coming as it did at the end of a summer of record-breaking temperatures, including in the Himalayas, ought to focus minds. Scientists have warned for years of the devastating consequences of melting glaciers, particularly for the millions of people who rely on them for water. But as well as a spur to accelerate the green transition and intensify decarbonisation, the plight of the Nepali people should be a wake-up call to the governments and institutions that must find a way to make a global climate finance system work – including in the aftermath of disasters such as Nepal’s. Turkey, which hosts the next climate summit in November, has positioned itself as a champion for developing countries. Boosting the loss and damage fund must be prioritised at those talks if climate justice is to remain a credible goal.

title: Lawmakers call for greater preparedness, relief for flood-hit Gegayling Tibetan settlement in Nepal - Phayul
description: Lawmakers call for greater preparedness, relief for flood-hit Gegayling Tibetan settlement in Nepal  Phayul
publisher.title: Phayul
full_article:
Tenzin Nyidon

DHARAMSHALA, Sept. 17: Members of the 18th Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile on Thursday called for greater preparedness and contingency planning for Tibetans in Nepal following the devastating August flash flood that caused extensive destruction in Nepal’s Rasuwa bordering Tibet where the Tibetan community in Gegayling settlement was severely affected.

Concerns were raised during the ongoing second session of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, as lawmakers discussed the disaster’s impact and the Central Tibetan Administration’s response. Parliamentarians extended condolences to families affected by the disaster and enquired about the CTA’s response, particularly plans for relief, rehabilitation, and reconstruction.

MP Tashi Dhondup specifically drew attention to what he described as a challenging political environment for Tibetans in Nepal, referring to discussions in the Nepalese Parliament and statements by former Nepalese home ministers that, according to him, included calls for the removal or expulsion of Tibetans from the country. Against this backdrop, he urged Tibetan representatives in Nepal to strengthen their preparedness and establish a coordinated mechanism for responding to future emergencies. He said local representatives of the CTA’s Department of Home had recently held meetings to assess the situation and sought updates and reports from the ground.

Responding to the MP, CTA Home Minister Palden Dhondup said the Department of Home initiated an emergency response as soon as it received information about the disaster. The department contacted its local representatives in Nepal and instructed them to assess immediate requirements and submit a financial estimate for emergency assistance. The initial estimate stood at ₹5 lakh, but was subsequently revised upward, with ₹7 lakh eventually dispatched for emergency relief.

The minister said the assistance was intended as an initial intervention, as the full scale of casualties and property damage could not be estimated immediately. “At this stage, we do not yet know exactly how many people have died or the extent of the damage to property and belongings,” he said. He added that a more comprehensive assessment would follow as information from the affected areas became available.

The Home Minister also disclosed that 14 people connected to the Tibetan community were initially unaccounted for. Of these, 11 were under the jurisdiction of a local Tibetan representative, while two boys, approximately 19 and 13 years old, had travelled from Kathmandu towards the affected area and were also reported missing. Another young man from a Tibetan settlement in southern India, who had reportedly moved to Nepal and married a Nepali woman, was likewise among those whose whereabouts were unknown. The minister cautioned against prematurely assuming that those missing had died, stressing that confirmation could take considerable time amid the scale of destruction and disrupted communications.

He said the Government of Nepal had extended rescue and relief assistance to Tibetans without discrimination, with necessary facilities made available to those affected. He said Tibetan representatives on the ground had been instructed to address immediate requirements while simultaneously developing longer-term plans for rehabilitation and reconstruction. They were also asked to identify needs for food and other essential supplies. Beyond preliminary assessments, the Department of Home plans to engage professionals to undertake a detailed evaluation of damaged houses, water-related destruction, infrastructure and other property before preparing a standardised reconstruction estimate, he said.

Minister Dhondup further said the department had received reports that some children affected by the disaster may have lost one or both parents and could face difficulties continuing their education. However, he said most of the cases identified so far appeared to concern the local Nepali population, and the department did not yet have a verified figure for Tibetan children in such circumstances. He said the information would be further cross-checked before definitive figures were released. The minister also emphasised that reconstruction should not be based solely on preliminary estimates submitted by local representatives, but should follow a systematic and professional damage assessment.

Beyond the immediate disaster response, the Home Minister’s intervention placed the flood within a wider discussion about the vulnerability of Tibetans living in Nepal. He said the CTA has been monitoring developments in Nepal closely while attempting to avoid actions that could further complicate the circumstances of Tibetans living there. The Home Minister said the Department’s approach was to continue supporting Tibetans in Nepal while recognising the political sensitivities surrounding their presence in the country.

title: Climate change contributed to Nepal rock-ice avalanche: scientists - Everest Chronicle
description: Climate change contributed to Nepal rock-ice avalanche: scientists  Everest Chronicle
publisher.title: Everest Chronicle
full_article:
A catastrophic rock-and-ice avalanche that triggered devastating floods along Nepal's border with China last month was made more likely by global warming, which weakened glaciers and mountain permafrost, an international team of scientists said Thursday.

The assessment, one of the first comprehensive scientific studies of the August 26 catastrophe, found that climate change was a destabilising factor acting on a mountain slope already vulnerable because of its underlying geology.

The disaster began when about two square kilometres of rock wall and glacier ice collapsed from Langtang Lirung at an altitude of about 5,150 metres.

The collapsing mass plunged roughly 1,400 metres to the valley floor, releasing energy equivalent to a magnitude 5.5 earthquake and producing seismic waves initially detected as an earthquake-like signal.

The avalanche rapidly transformed into a debris flood, carrying rock, ice, sediment and water down the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.

The torrent reached the Rasuwagadhi border, about 22 kilometres downstream, in seven minutes, travelling at an average speed of 188 kilometres per hour, the researchers said.

It then swept through Timure and Syabrubesi before reaching the Trishuli valley and devastating communities including Betrawati and Trishuli Bazaar.

The flood travelled about 200 kilometres to Devghat in less than seven hours, where river discharge more than doubled to about 5,850 cubic metres per second. Around 30.5 million cubic metres of sediment and debris were deposited along the disaster corridor.

Nepal's disaster authorities had recorded more than 1,300 deaths and more than 5,000 people missing by September 14, while thousands more had been rescued or treated.

The international team included researchers from Nepal, Pakistan, Britain, Ireland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, the United States, New Zealand and the Netherlands, with expertise ranging from glaciology and mountain hydrology to climate science and seismology.

The scientists said the geological structure ultimately controlled where and how the slope failed, while several factors may have contributed to its instability.

A magnitude 7.8 earthquake in 2015 triggered another major rock-and-ice avalanche in the Langtang region and may have weakened the mountain's underlying rock mass over the longer term, although its specific contribution to the 2026 collapse could not yet be established.

The researchers also identified warming temperatures, permafrost degradation, glacier thinning and changing precipitation patterns as potential contributing factors.

Glaciers in the region have been losing more than half a metre in thickness each year, while the retreat of the Langtang-Lirung glacier has accelerated since 2010.

The freezing level has also risen by about 100 metres per decade in recent decades during the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons, increasing the potential for permafrost thaw and glacier loss.

July and August 2026 were unusually warm around the disaster site. The researchers found that human-caused climate change had increased temperatures during those months by about 1.5 degrees Celsius compared with a climate 1.4C cooler than today.

But the scientists stressed that they had not determined whether the avalanche would have occurred without human-caused climate change.

Instead, they said climate change should be understood as a factor that can increase instability in already vulnerable mountain terrain.

The assessment also concluded that the disaster was beyond the design and predictive limits of existing warning systems, highlighting the difficulty of protecting communities from extremely rapid and cascading mountain hazards.

It called for stronger high-altitude monitoring, earth observation, risk communication and data sharing between countries, alongside greater support for communities facing climate-related loss and damage.
